bill.title: To clarify the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, to appropriately limit the application of defenses based on the passage of time and other non-merits defenses to claims under that Act.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
subjects: War crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity

industries.rationale: The bill expands litigation procedures, jurisdictional reach, and limits defenses in civil claims, directly affecting law firms handling art recovery and international litigation.
Museums and cultural institutions holding artwork are subject to expanded liability and jurisdictional reach under the modified claims procedures.

bill.plainSummary: This bill removes the 2026 deadline for filing lawsuits to recover art and property stolen during the Holocaust, allowing claims to be filed indefinitely as long as they are brought within six years of discovering the item. It makes it easier to sue foreign governments in U.S. courts and to serve legal papers on defendants anywhere in the country. The bill also blocks certain legal defenses, such as arguments that too much time has passed or that U.S. courts should defer to foreign laws, for both current and future cases.

bill.title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to the authority of Congress and the States to regulate contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections and to enact public financing systems for political campaigns.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The amendment would directly regulate how advocacy organizations raise and spend money to influence elections.
The amendment would reshape campaign-finance law and likely generate substantial litigation and compliance work for law firms and lobbying practices.
Regulations on election-related spending could affect advertising revenue and the market for political communications services.
New restrictions on corporate election spending and potential public financing systems could affect financial institutions' political engagement and compliance obligations.

bill.plainSummary: This proposed constitutional amendment would allow Congress and state legislatures to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit them to create public financing systems for campaigns and to treat corporations differently from individual people, including by prohibiting corporations from spending money on elections. The amendment would give lawmakers the authority to write laws implementing these changes.

bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and in addition to the Committees on Rules, Armed Services, the Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: The bill fundamentally restructures the governance of the District, creating a new state government and redefining the federal district.
Statehood would change property tax authority and land-use regulation for most of the current District, affecting developers and property owners.
The transition of DC courts, judicial proceedings, and contractual obligations to state authority would affect legal practice and litigation in the new jurisdiction.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would admit most of the current District of Columbia as the 51st state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, with two senators and one representative in Congress. A small federal district containing the Capitol, White House, Supreme Court, and nearby monuments would remain as the seat of the federal government. The bill sets up a transition process for DC laws, courts, contracts, and obligations to continue under state authority, and creates a commission to manage the shift to statehood.

bill.title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States providing that the rights protected and extended by the Constitution are the rights of natural persons only.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
bill.policyArea: Civil Rights and Liberties, Minority Issues

industries.rationale: The amendment would subject banks and financial firms to new constitutional limits on political spending and strip them of constitutional rights currently recognized for corporations.
Technology companies would lose constitutional protections as corporate entities and face new restrictions on election-related expenditures and contributions.
Oil, gas, and coal companies would be subject to campaign finance limits and lose constitutional rights currently available to corporate entities.
Pharmaceutical and device manufacturers would face new restrictions on political spending and lose constitutional protections as artificial entities.
Law firms and lobbying organizations would operate under new campaign finance regulations and potentially altered constitutional frameworks for corporate clients.
Media corporations would lose constitutional rights as artificial entities, potentially affecting their ability to make election-related expenditures and editorial decisions.

bill.plainSummary: This proposed constitutional amendment would establish that only individual human beings—not corporations or other artificial entities—hold rights under the Constitution. It would require all levels of government to regulate or limit campaign contributions and spending, including candidates' own funds, to ensure equal political access regardless of wealth. The amendment would also mandate public disclosure of all permitted contributions and prevent courts from treating campaign spending as protected speech under the First Amendment.

bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 59.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content-moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on platforms that host user-generated content.
Online publishers and digital media platforms may face compliance obligations if they host user-generated intimate content.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. It would require websites and apps that host user-generated content to remove such images within 48 hours of being notified by the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

bill.title: Safe Schools Improvement Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

industries.rationale: The bill imposes new policy, reporting, and grievance-procedure obligations on local educational agencies and state education systems.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require states to ensure that local school districts adopt policies prohibiting bullying and harassment of students based on race, color, national origin, disability, religion, sex (including sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex traits). School districts would need to notify students and parents annually about these policies, establish complaint procedures, and publicly report data on bullying incidents. The Department of Education would evaluate anti-bullying programs every two years, and the National Center for Education Statistics would collect nationwide data on these incidents.

The bill would allow state and local governments to use federal grant funds to operate buy-back programs for these firearms and magazines.

bill.title: Scientific Integrity Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

industries.rationale: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies conduct and rely on federally funded research subject to these integrity requirements.
Federal research on climate, emissions, and energy impacts this sector's regulatory environment and public discourse.
Federal research on energy technologies and climate directly affects this sector's market and policy landscape.
Agricultural research conducted or funded by USDA and other agencies would be subject to these integrity standards.
Universities receive federal research funding and would need to comply with integrity policies in their federally supported work.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require every federal agency that funds, conducts, or oversees scientific research to create and enforce a policy protecting scientific integrity. These policies must ensure that research conclusions are not influenced by political considerations, prohibit suppression or alteration of findings, and allow researchers to share their work. Each agency would need to appoint a Scientific Integrity Officer, establish a complaint process, provide training, and submit its policy to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy for approval.
